claim: Swapping `mayOutputUndefined` for `mayOmitUndefined` in the `hasConditionalKeys` predicate can desynchronize this gate from the per-key emission logic further down, silently dropping the conditional-inclusion code path for keys that still need it.
rationale: `hasConditionalKeys` is a summary flag that decides whether the generated object literal needs the slower per-key conditional construction. Its predicate must be a superset of (or exactly match) whatever condition each individual key's emission code uses to decide 'include only if present / only if not undefined'. If any downstream site still tests `mayOutputUndefined(...)` (or `!== undefined`) per key while this gate now tests the narrower `mayOmitUndefined(...)`, the fast path will be selected for a schema that actually contains a conditional key, producing wrong output (e.g. an `undefined` key emitted that should have been omitted, or vice versa). I could not inspect the rest of the file to confirm both predicates were updated together, so this is a medium-confidence concern that is worth verifying at every other use of `mayOutputUndefined` in this function.

claim: The narrower predicate is an observable behavior change for defaulted/required keys whose output is `undefined`: such keys will now always be written into the result object instead of being conditionally omitted.
rationale: The replacement comment states 'defaulted required outputs keep their keys even when undefined', which implies `mayOmitUndefined` returns false for keys that previously made `mayOutputUndefined` return true. Any schema consisting solely of such keys flips from the conditional-construction path to the unconditional one, so the parsed result gains own properties with value `undefined` where it previously had none. That is visible to callers via `Object.keys`, `in`, spread, and deep-equality assertions, and it also changes JSON serialization. If intentional it should be matched by tests; if not, it is a regression. Medium confidence — it depends entirely on the exact semantics of the two helpers.

claim: The removed comment documented the key-ordering contract (shape keys in declared order, then unknown keys in for...in order) and the middle-rung inclusion rule; replacing it with a one-line note about defaults loses the invariant that the surrounding code still depends on.
rationale: Strictly a comment change and therefore low priority, but flagged because the deleted text described the precise inclusion rule that the modified predicate implements. If the rule itself changed, the new comment is incomplete; if it did not change, useful documentation of a subtle invariant was dropped. Low confidence that this affects behavior at all.

claim: `issue.options` is not a property of the `invalid_union` issue type in Zod v4 (union issues carry `errors`, a nested array of issue arrays; `options` belongs to `invalid_value`/enum-style issues). This guard therefore likely never passes, making the discriminator message — the very string being edited in this diff — dead code.
rationale: If the runtime issue object has no `options`, the reworded branch can never be reached and the locale silently falls through to the generic "Вуруди нодуруст". It also implies an unsafe/implicit access on a union-typed issue. Medium confidence — depends on the exact `$ZodIssueInvalidUnion` shape in this version, but other locales in this package do not key off `issue.options` for `invalid_union`.

claim: `${o}` interpolates each option with default string conversion; non-primitive options (objects, or nested issue arrays if `options` ever is populated) render as `'[object Object]'`.
rationale: Produces a useless user-facing message for any non-string/number option. Other locales typically use `util.joinValues` / `util.stringifyPrimitive` for this reason. Medium-high confidence that raw interpolation is wrong here.

claim: The message is hardcoded to talk about a "discriminator" even though the branch is reached for any `invalid_union` issue, not just discriminated unions.
rationale: A plain (non-discriminated) union failure would produce a message referring to a discriminator that does not exist, which is misleading to end users. The diff rewords this string without addressing the mismatch. Low-medium confidence, since it depends on whether `options` is ever populated for plain unions.

claim: try/finally restores `indent` but does not roll back content already written by the throwing callback, so the doc can still be left in a half-written/inconsistent state
rationale: The fix addresses only one half of the failure mode described in the comment: if `fn` calls `doc.write(...)` several times and then throws, those lines stay in `this.content` at the deeper indentation while the caller continues writing at the outer indent. If the intent is that the compiler can keep using this doc after a child throws, the emitted output may contain a truncated/partial block (e.g. an opened `if (` with no closing brace). Medium confidence — depends on whether callers tolerate partial output; if they do not, an additional content checkpoint/rollback (record `this.content.length` before `fn` and truncate in the `finally` on failure) would be needed.

claim: `indented` is synchronous-only; a callback returning a promise would decrement the indent before the async work runs
rationale: `fn` is typed `(doc: Doc) => void`, so an `async` callback still type-checks (its `Promise<void>` return is assignable to `void`). With the new `finally`, the indent is restored as soon as the synchronous part returns, and any writes performed after the first `await` land at the wrong indentation with the rejection unhandled. This was equally true before the change, but the `try/finally` makes it look exception-safe. Low confidence that any caller does this — worth a quick check of usages.

claim: Switching `buckets` from `Map` to `WeakMap` drops `size`, `clear()`, `forEach()` and iteration; any existing code in this module that inspects or resets the bucket map will break.
rationale: `WeakMap` is not a structural superset of `Map`. Memoizer implementations commonly do `state.buckets.clear()` at the end of a parse, read `.size`, or iterate buckets to flush pending issues. I cannot see the rest of the file, so this is a suspicion rather than a confirmed break, but it is the most likely fallout of this type change and deserves verification.

claim: Making the per-node bucket weak allows memo entries to be garbage collected mid-parse, so memoization becomes non-deterministic; an `Entry` whose `issues` is still `null` (children not yet parsed) can disappear if the only strong reference to its key object was the map itself.
rationale: With a strong `Map` the entry was guaranteed to survive the whole parse. With a `WeakMap` the entry's lifetime is tied to the key object's reachability. If keys are transient wrapper/marker objects created per visit rather than caller-owned data, a GC-triggered miss changes behavior (recomputation, duplicated issues, or an undetected cycle). Moderate confidence: safe only if every key stays strongly reachable for the whole parse.

claim: The new comment states the bucket is cached on the schema instance and "outlives the parse", which means memo entries keyed by a data object are now reused across separate parse calls with different contexts.
rationale: An `Entry` carries `issues` produced under one parse's context (error map, path prefix, config). If the same object graph is parsed twice against the same schema, a cross-parse memo hit could return issues computed under the previous context. The strong `Map` was presumably per-parse state, so this is a behavior change callers could be surprised by. Confidence moderate — depends on how `attach` scopes the bucket, which is not visible in this hunk.

claim: `backEdges` as a `WeakSet` can no longer be iterated, sized, or cleared, and its membership can silently shrink under GC.
rationale: Back-edge tracking usually needs a drain/clear step once a cycle resolves (e.g., walking recorded nodes to propagate issues). `WeakSet` supports only `add`/`has`/`delete`, so such logic breaks. A node dropped by GC would also silently stop being reported as a back-edge. Same caveat: consuming code is not visible here.

claim: `WeakMap`/`WeakSet` throw `TypeError` on non-object keys, whereas `Map`/`Set` accepted anything; if any key reaching this state is a primitive (or a registered symbol) at runtime, the memoizer now throws instead of just memoizing.
rationale: The declared key type is `object`, so this only bites if a cast or `any` lets a primitive through — plausible in a parser walking arbitrary input. Low confidence, but the failure mode changes from benign to a thrown exception, so it is cheap to check the call sites that write into `buckets`/`backEdges`.

claim: Exclusive bounds (`bag.exclusiveMinimum` / `bag.exclusiveMaximum`) are ignored by the new narrowing logic, so a tighter exclusive bound set by `.gt()`/`.lt()` does not prevent the format range from being written.
rationale: The sibling `$ZodCheckGreaterThan`/`$ZodCheckLessThan` attach handlers distinguish inclusive vs exclusive and store into separate bag fields. Here only `bag.minimum`/`bag.maximum` are consulted, so `z.number().gt(-5).int()` still ends up with `minimum = -9007199254740991` alongside `exclusiveMinimum = -5`, i.e. the stated goal ("don't overwrite bounds an earlier check stored") is only half-implemented. Downstream consumers that take only one of the two fields (e.g. JSON Schema emission) can report a looser bound than intended. Moderate confidence — the exact bag field names depend on the version of the gt/lt checks in this file.

claim: NaN bounds silently discard the format range: if a prior check stored `NaN` in `bag.minimum`/`bag.maximum`, both comparisons are false and the format's real bound is never recorded.
rationale: `minimum > NaN` and `maximum < NaN` are both `false`, so `bag.minimum` stays `NaN` and the int32/safeint range is lost from the bag entirely (previously it was always written). Reachable via `z.number().min(NaN).int()`. Low-impact edge case but it is a behavior regression versus the unconditional assignment, and the bag is what schema-introspection/JSON-Schema code reads.

claim: The `as number` casts hide a possible `number | bigint` bag value, and mixed-type comparison would silently change which bound wins.
rationale: `bag.minimum`/`bag.maximum` are typed to accept `bigint` as well (shared with the bigint-format/length checks). Casting to `number` suppresses the type error rather than handling it; at runtime a `bigint` compares fine with `>`/`<` but the written value type then becomes inconsistent (mixed number/bigint bounds on one bag). For a pure number-format check this is probably unreachable, so confidence that it bites in practice is low, but the unchecked cast is worth a second look.

claim: Behavior change: `bag.minimum`/`bag.maximum` no longer reliably describe the numeric format's representable range, which may surprise consumers that read them to learn the format bounds.
rationale: Before, these fields always equaled `util.NUMBER_FORMAT_RANGES[def.format]`. After the change they can hold an arbitrary user-supplied bound, so any code that introspects the bag to recover the format's width (mock/faker generation, range-based optimizations, tests asserting `int32().._zod.bag.minimum === -2147483648`) will now see different values depending on check ordering. Likely intentional for JSON Schema output, but it is an observable API-surface change worth calling out; existing snapshot tests on `_zod.bag` are the most likely breakage.

claim: `strip()` relies on the key `catchall` being present-with-value-`undefined` to clear an existing catchall; if `util.mergeDefs` skips `undefined` values (a very common merge-helper behavior) `strip()` silently becomes a no-op on a schema that already has a catchall (e.g. `z.object({}).strict().strip()` would stay strict).
rationale: The old spread `{ ...def, catchall: undefined }` always defines the own property `catchall` with value `undefined`, which overrides the inherited/previous value. Whether `mergeDefs` preserves that depends entirely on its implementation: if it copies property descriptors (Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors + defineProperties) the behavior is preserved, but if it filters `undefined` or uses a `value ?? existing` style merge, the semantics change. This is the only call site in the hunk whose correctness hinges on undefined-preservation, so it deserves an explicit check/test. Moderate confidence that this is at least worth verifying; low-to-moderate that it is an actual bug.

claim: Copying a lazily-defined `shape` accessor onto a fresh def object can defeat the lazy cache: the lazy getter typically caches by assigning back to the *original* def object it closed over, so the copied accessor on the merged def re-invokes the resolver on every access instead of once.
rationale: If `mergeDefs` works by transplanting property descriptors, an accessor created by a `defineLazy`-style helper closes over the original object; writing the cached value there does not replace the accessor on the new object. The stated goal of the change (avoid minting a fresh subtree) could then be inverted — resolution happens on every read of `newDef.shape` rather than once. I'm not fully certain of the helper's implementation, but this is the classic failure mode of descriptor-copying merges over lazy props and is worth confirming with a test that reads `.shape` twice on a `.catchall()`-derived schema and asserts referential equality.

claim: Replacing the object-literal spread with `util.mergeDefs(...)` likely loses compile-time checking of the def shape, so typos or wrong-typed fields in the second argument would no longer be caught.
rationale: Generic merge helpers commonly return `Record<string, any>` or a loosely inferred intersection, and `this.clone()` then accepts it without validating keys. The previous literal was structurally checked against the def type. Low severity but a real reduction in type safety across all five call sites; flagged once here.

claim: `mergeDefs` returns a new object whose prototype/own-property flags may differ from the plain object produced by a spread (e.g. properties defined via `Object.defineProperties` default to non-enumerable/non-writable when descriptors are constructed manually), which could break downstream code that enumerates or mutates `def`.
rationale: Spread always yields enumerable, writable, configurable own data properties. Any descriptor-based construction risks differing attributes, which matters for code that does `{...def}`, `JSON.stringify(def)`, `Object.keys(def)`, or reassigns `def.catchall` later. I have not read the helper, so this is speculative, but it is a plausible source of subtle behavior change for existing callers.

claim: min/maxProperties are enforced via a post-parse check on the Zod object's *output*, so keys stripped by the object schema are not counted
rationale: `checkObjectGuards` is layered on top of `zodSchema`, which at this point is usually a `ZodObject`. Unless `additionalProperties` forced `.passthrough()`, Zod strips unknown keys before the check runs, so `{a:1, b:2, c:3}` against `{type:'object', properties:{a}, maxProperties:1}` would see only `{a:1}` and pass, and `minProperties` would likewise under-count. JSON Schema counts properties on the raw instance. Unless `checkObjectGuards` internally uses the raw input (can't tell from this hunk), this is a correctness bug. Medium confidence.

claim: `typeof x === "number"` accepts NaN, Infinity, negative and non-integer values for min/maxProperties
rationale: A malformed schema with `minProperties: NaN` or `-1` (or `1.5`) yields `!== undefined`, so the guard is installed with a nonsensical bound — `NaN` comparisons make every object fail (or every object pass, depending on the comparison direction) silently. Consider validating `Number.isInteger(v) && v >= 0`. Also `minProperties: 0` is a no-op that now needlessly wraps the schema in a check.

claim: Schemas with only min/maxProperties are now wrapped, losing ZodObject-specific methods and possibly surprising existing callers
rationale: Previously a `type: 'object'` schema with `minProperties`/`maxProperties` converted to a plain `ZodObject` (the constraints were ignored); now it returns whatever `checkObjectGuards` produces. If that wrapper is not a `ZodObject` (e.g. a `ZodType` with `.check()`/`.superRefine()` or a pipe), downstream users who call `.extend()`, `.shape`, `.partial()`, or who rely on `instanceof ZodObject`, will break. Worth confirming `checkObjectGuards` preserves the object instance (e.g. via `.check()` which returns the same class) rather than widening the type.

claim: No sanity check for `minProperties > maxProperties`, producing a silently unsatisfiable schema
rationale: Both bounds are forwarded verbatim; a contradictory pair yields a schema that rejects everything with a confusing error instead of surfacing a conversion-time problem. Low severity, but the converter elsewhere tends to report unsupported/invalid constructs.

claim: The TODO noting that `uniqueItems` and `contains`/`minContains`/`maxContains` are unsupported is deleted, but the array branch in this hunk is otherwise unchanged
rationale: If those keywords were implemented elsewhere in this change the removal is fine; if not, the deletion hides a known gap where those constraints are silently dropped (validation becomes more permissive than the source schema). Worth verifying the array conversion actually handles them now.

claim: `import * as regexes from "./regexes.js"` is a runtime (value) import, unlike every other import in this file's header, which is type-only. This introduces a real module dependency from json-schema-processors into regexes and could create a circular import or unexpected bundle growth.
rationale: All neighboring imports are `import type`, so this file previously had (almost) no runtime deps on the sibling modules. Adding a value import means regexes.js is now evaluated whenever this module loads. If regexes.js (or anything it transitively pulls in) imports back into the core schema graph, this can produce a TDZ/undefined-at-module-init problem that only manifests at runtime in certain bundlers. Worth confirming regexes.js is dependency-free and that the imported regex objects are only read lazily inside functions, not at module top level. Confidence: low-to-moderate — regexes.js is typically leaf-level in zod, so this is likely fine, but the asymmetry with the other imports is worth a second look.

claim: Newly imported `type Seen` may be unused or may indicate the file now depends on internal to-JSON-Schema traversal state that it previously did not.
rationale: The hunk only shows the import being added; if `Seen` is not actually referenced in the rest of the file, it is dead (harmless but noise under `noUnusedLocals`, which would fail the build). More importantly, if it *is* used, it means processors now reach into per-node traversal/cycle-tracking state — a behavior-relevant coupling worth verifying that callers pass a consistent `Seen` and that mutation of it doesn't leak across separate `toJSONSchema` invocations. Confidence: low, since the hunk doesn't show the usage site.

claim: The new lookahead accepts a lone U+20E3 (combining enclosing keycap) or a single Regional Indicator as the "anchor", so strings that are still not valid emoji pass validation.
rationale: `⃣` and Regional Indicators are themselves `\p{Emoji_Component}`, so they satisfy both the lookahead and the main character class. `emoji().test("⃣")` (a bare keycap with no digit/#/* base) and `emoji().test("\u{1F1FA}")` (a single regional indicator, i.e. half a flag) both return true. The stated goal of the lookahead is to require an anchor because components are "not an emoji without a base", but these two anchors have exactly the same base-less problem. Reasonably confident; easy to verify in a REPL.

claim: The fix only requires one pictograph/RI/keycap somewhere in the string; arbitrary ASCII digits, `#`, `*`, ZWJ and variation selectors are still accepted alongside it.
rationale: Because the lookahead is `(?=[\s\S]*...)` and the body class is unchanged, inputs like "\u{1F600}123", "#*\u{1F600}" or "\u{1F600}‍‍‍" still match. The comment implies digits/#/* are no longer acceptable, but they are only rejected when no pictograph appears anywhere in the string. Incomplete fix if the intent was to reject stray components. High confidence on the behavior.

claim: Behavior change: inputs that previously validated (e.g. "123", "#", "*", a lone skin-tone modifier, a lone ZWJ) now fail, which is a breaking change for existing callers.
rationale: This is presumably the intended fix, but `z.string().emoji()` consumers relying on the old looser acceptance will start seeing validation errors, with no version gate or changelog note visible in this hunk. Worth confirming existing emoji test fixtures are updated and that this lands in a suitable release.

claim: `\p{Regional_Indicator}` is a less commonly used Unicode binary property; on an engine that does not recognize it, `new RegExp(_emoji, "u")` throws a SyntaxError at call time rather than at module load.
rationale: Because `emoji()` builds the RegExp lazily, an unsupported property name would surface as a runtime SyntaxError inside user validation. Both properties are ES2018 and supported by modern engines, so this is probably fine, but worth checking against the library's minimum engine/browser support. Low confidence this is an actual problem.

claim: `ctx.intersections.push(allOf)` assumes `intersections` is always present and initialized on the processor context; if it is optional or omitted by any context-construction path, this throws a TypeError during schema conversion.
rationale: Only the hunk is visible, so I cannot confirm the context type. If `intersections` is declared optional (`intersections?: ...[]`) or any ctx literal (nested conversion, tests, alternate `toJSONSchema` entry points) omits it, the new unguarded `push` is a hard runtime failure on any intersection schema. Moderate confidence this deserves verification.

claim: When a child intersection is flattened via `...(a.allOf as any[])`, that child's array was already pushed onto `ctx.intersections` but is now detached from the output, so `finalize` will fold it a second time over element references shared with the new `allOf`.
rationale: The spread copies element references, not the array, so both the parent array and the orphaned child array contain the same member schema objects. If folding mutates members in place (implied by 'finalize folds every object holding it'), the same members get merged twice, which can produce a wrong schema or duplicated keys. Reasonably confident this is at least redundant work and plausibly a correctness bug.

claim: Registering the array (rather than the owning schema object) leaves a stale entry if `json.allOf` is later replaced by an `override` callback, a `$ref`/`$defs` extraction, or an io-specific rewrite: the orphaned array is folded and the live one is not.
rationale: The added comment explicitly relies on the array identity being shared with every wrapper, which makes replacement of `json.allOf` anywhere downstream silently skip folding. Lower confidence since it depends on whether overrides can replace `allOf`, but the failure mode would be silent.

claim: `$ZodNumberFormats` is referenced unqualified while every other core type in this block uses the `core.` namespace prefix; if the corresponding import was not added, this is a compile error.
rationale: The surrounding code consistently uses `core.$ZodNumberFormatInternals`, `core.$ZodNumberParams`, etc. The hunk header (1193 -> 1194) suggests a line was added above, likely the import, but the import is not visible in this hunk, so I can't confirm. Medium confidence that it is fine, but worth verifying that `$ZodNumberFormats` is actually imported (and exported from core) rather than silently resolving to something else.

claim: The runtime `ZodNumberFormat` constructor is still typed as the non-generic/default `core.$constructor<ZodNumberFormat>` (i.e. `Format = $ZodNumberFormats`), so it cannot preserve the concrete format of the value it constructs.
rationale: Because the constructor value's type always widens to the full format union, every factory below now needs an unchecked assertion. Making the declared constructor type generic (or having `core._int`/`_float32`/... be typed to return the narrow format) would let the compiler verify the mapping instead of trusting the casts. Confident this is why the casts were needed; severity is design/maintainability, not a runtime bug.

claim: The newly added `as ZodInt` / `as ZodFloat32` / ... assertions silence the only check that the declared literal format matches what the core `_int`/`_float32`/... helpers actually set at runtime.
rationale: `int()` is now declared as `ZodNumberFormat<"safeint">`, but the assertion means nothing verifies that `core._int` really sets `format: "safeint"` (zod core has both `"safeint"` and `"int32"`). If any of the five helpers set a different format string, the declared type silently lies and downstream narrowing on `_zod.def.format` breaks with no compile error. Please double-check each literal against the corresponding `core._*` implementation. Reported once here; the same concern applies identically to the float32/float64/int32/uint32 casts.

claim: Parameterizing `ZodNumberFormat` makes `ZodInt`, `ZodFloat32`, `ZodInt32`, etc. mutually non-assignable, which is a breaking type change for existing callers.
rationale: Previously all five interfaces were structurally identical (`extends ZodNumberFormat {}`), so user code such as `const s: ZodFloat32 = z.float64()`, or arrays/ternaries mixing them, type-checked. With distinct `Format` arguments those now error or infer unions. This is likely the intended improvement, but it is a semver-visible type break worth calling out in release notes. Moderate confidence on the assignability consequence, depending on whether `Format` actually appears in `$ZodNumberFormatInternals`.

claim: The new `!omittableOnInput` guard is placed on the outer `if`, so it skips the entire block, not just the `required` assignment.
rationale: The stated intent (and the comment above) is only that the key set should not be *required* on input. If the body of `if (keyValues && !def.partial) { ... if (validKeyValues.length > 0) { ... } }` does anything besides `json.required = ...` — e.g. emits per-key `properties`, `propertyNames`, or tightens `additionalProperties` — that schema tightening is now silently dropped for input schemas whose value type is optional-in, which would let arbitrary/invalid keys through on input. If the block only assigns `required`, this is a non-issue. Medium confidence; depends on code below line 492 that isn't shown.

claim: `inputOptin(...) !== undefined` assumes the helper returns `undefined` for non-optional inputs; if it can return a non-optional sentinel (e.g. `"required"`), the condition is inverted-ish and would suppress `required` for every record.
rationale: In zod core `_zod.optin` is typed `"optional" | undefined`, so `!== undefined` is probably right, but a resolver helper could normalize to a string union including a non-optional value. Comparing explicitly against `"optional"` would be safer and self-documenting. Low-to-medium confidence — worth a quick check of `inputOptin`'s signature. Also note this call is evaluated unconditionally, even when `keyValues` is undefined or `def.partial` is true, which is wasted work and, for lazy/recursive value types, could trigger resolution (or recursion) that previously never happened on this path.

claim: Unsafe cast `def.valueType as schemas.$ZodType` may be hiding a real type mismatch.
rationale: `$ZodRecord`'s `valueType` should already be a `$ZodType`; needing a cast suggests either the def is typed loosely (e.g. `unknown`/`SomeType`) or `inputOptin` expects a narrower shape. If `valueType` can be undefined for some record variants, `inputOptin` would receive `undefined` and could throw at runtime. Low confidence without the surrounding type declarations, but casts in this position are a common source of latent nullability bugs.

claim: Gating on `ctx.io === "input"` only considers the global/current IO direction, not a direction flip introduced by an enclosing pipe/transform.
rationale: If `ctx.io` is mutated/threaded as the walker descends (as is typical when a `$ZodPipe` swaps input/output perspectives), reading it here is correct; if it is a fixed top-level option while the effective direction for this subtree differs, the `required` list will be wrong in nested pipe cases. Low confidence — depends on how `ctx.io` is maintained elsewhere in this file; worth confirming against how other processors consume it.

claim: The new constraint no longer guarantees `Shape extends core.$ZodShape`, so `core.$InferObjectInput<Shape, {}>` on line 2847 may no longer satisfy its own type-parameter constraint (and can see `undefined` values).
rationale: The mapped type `{ [k in keyof T as ...]?: core.$ZodType<unknown, T[k]> }` produces *optional* members, whose type is `core.$ZodType<unknown, T[k]> | undefined`, and its keys can be `symbol`/`number` (anything in `keyof T`). `$ZodShape` is (in zod v4 core) `Record<string, $ZodType>`. A `Shape` inferred under the new constraint therefore does not necessarily extend `$ZodShape`, which will either be a hard compile error at the `$InferObjectInput<Shape, {}>` usage or silently infer `undefined`-valued properties into the result type. Fairly confident this needs an explicit `& core.$ZodShape` intersection on the constraint.

claim: Restricting shape keys to `keyof T` makes the `T & core.$InferObjectInput<Shape, {}>` return type pointless and breaks callers that used `.properties()` to declare properties not statically present on `T`.
rationale: The return type intersects `T` with the inferred shape, which only has meaning if the shape can introduce keys `T` does not already have (the common use case: `z.instanceof(SomeOpaqueClass).properties({ extra: z.string() })`). With a mapped-type constraint keyed on `keyof T`, object-literal excess-property checking rejects any key outside `keyof T`, so that usage is now a compile error. This is a behavior/API regression for existing callers; confident about the excess-property rejection, less so about how widely it was used.

claim: Excluding `Function`-typed members via `T[k] extends Function ? never : k` makes it impossible to validate any method/function-valued property at all, not merely absent from autocomplete.
rationale: The key remapping removes those keys from the constraint entirely, so passing e.g. `{ callback: z.custom<Function>() }` for a class whose `callback` is a function becomes an excess-property error. If the intent was only to avoid the `Object.prototype.toString` collision described in the comment, a narrower fix (e.g. only excluding keys that come from `Object.prototype`, or intersecting with `Partial<core.$ZodShape>`) would keep function props usable. Also note the exclusion misses union types like `(() => void) | undefined`, which do not extend `Function`, so the collision guard is inconsistent.

claim: For the default `T = unknown` (and the `core.$constructor<ZodInstanceOf>` declaration below), `keyof T` is `never`, so the shape constraint collapses to `{}` and accepts literally any argument, including non-schema values.
rationale: `{ [k in never as ...]?: ... }` is `{}`, which every non-null value is assignable to, so `properties({ foo: 123 })` type-checks on a `ZodInstanceOf<unknown>`. The previous `core.$ZodShape` constraint at least required schema values. Confident about the type-level behavior; severity depends on how often `T` is left unknown.

claim: Constraining the property schema by its *Input* parameter (`core.$ZodType<unknown, T[k]>`) rather than its Output checks the wrong side for transforming/coercing schemas.
rationale: `$ZodType<Output, Input>` — placing `T[k]` in the Input slot means a schema like `z.coerce.number()` (Input `unknown`) or `z.string().transform(Number)` (Input `string`) is matched against the declared property type rather than the value the check actually produces/validates. Given the stated goal ("a schema that can't accept the property's type is an error") Input may be intentional, but combined with the declared `out Input` variance this rejects wider-input schemas (e.g. `z.string()` for a prop typed `"a" | "b"`), which callers may find surprising. Moderate confidence — depends on the exact variance annotations in `$ZodType`.

Confidence is moderate: the leak risk is pre-existing, but this change makes the insertion path easier to spread.

claim: `impl` is still dereferenced without a null check, so a Blob not backed by a jsdom impl (cross-realm or subclassed Blob) throws a raw `TypeError` from inside the compat helper.
rationale: `(blob as any)[implSymbol]` is `undefined` for any Blob that did not come from this jsdom window; `impl._bytes` then throws "Cannot read properties of undefined". This is pre-existing behavior, but the change touched exactly this expression and introduced an `impl` local, so it is a cheap place to add `impl?.` plus a descriptive error. Low-to-medium confidence that such blobs actually reach this helper.

claim: Assumes jsdom 28's `_bytes` is a BufferSource with the same semantics as the old `_buffer`; if it is a `Uint8Array` view into a larger pooled ArrayBuffer, correctness depends on Node's Blob honoring byteOffset/byteLength.
rationale: Node's Blob constructor does respect the view's byteOffset/byteLength, so this is most likely fine, but the rename from `_buffer` (Node Buffer) to `_bytes` (likely Uint8Array) is a type change, not just a name change — worth confirming against the jsdom 28 implementation, and worth a test asserting blob byte equality for a non-trivial payload. Low confidence that this is an actual bug.

claim: The new `else if` branch silently forces `nextTick`/`queueMicrotask` into `toNotFake`, removing the only way a user could fake those two timers without enumerating every method in `toFake`.
rationale: Previously, `toNotFake: ['setTimeout']` (with `toFake` unset) meant everything except `setTimeout` was faked, including `nextTick` and `queueMicrotask`. After this change those two are always unfaked whenever `toFake` is undefined, so a user who deliberately wanted `process.nextTick` mocked via the `toNotFake` style config can no longer express that — they must switch to an explicit exhaustive `toFake` list. This may be the intended default-safety change, but it is a silent behavior change for existing callers and deserves a doc/changelog note. Confidence: high that behavior changes, medium on whether it's intentional.

claim: The `isChildProcess()` guard below is now dead code for the `toFake === undefined` path, and remains inconsistent for the `toFake !== undefined` path.
rationale: When `toFake` is undefined, `nextTick` is already appended to `toNotFake` by the new branch (or `toFake` excludes it), so the `!toNotFake.includes('nextTick')` check can never be true. The guard only still matters when the user supplied an explicit `toFake` *and* a `toNotFake`, i.e. the one case neither branch above handles — worth confirming that combination is still handled as intended. Low-to-medium confidence this matters functionally; mostly redundancy plus an untouched edge case.

claim: The `else if (toFake === undefined && toNotFake !== undefined)` condition contains a redundant second clause, and the loop reallocates the array on each iteration.
rationale: Inside the `else` of `toFake === undefined && toNotFake === undefined`, if `toFake === undefined` then `toNotFake` must be defined, so the extra check is dead (harmless, but may hide the intent). Additionally, `toNotFake = [...toNotFake, timer]` inside the loop copies the array up to twice; building a single new array would be clearer and avoids the transient allocation. Both are non-functional nits, reported only because they touch the changed control flow.

claim: Adding `uncheckedKey.startsWith(testName)` now requires the caller to pass the *full* snapshot key prefix (including any parent `describe` path), otherwise previously-cleaned keys will be reported as obsolete.
rationale: Snapshot keys are built as `<full test path> <n>` or `<full test path> > <hint> <n>`. Previously the regex was applied to `slice(testName.length)` without verifying the prefix, so it happened to match loosely even when `testName` was not the actual prefix. If any caller passes only the leaf test name (or a name normalized/trimmed differently from how the key was generated — e.g. different whitespace or a `>`-joined path), the `startsWith` guard now fails and those snapshots will be marked unchecked/obsolete and potentially removed on `--update`. Worth verifying every call site passes the exact key prefix. Moderate confidence — the change is likely intentional and a bug fix for the false-positive direction, but it introduces a new false-negative direction.

claim: Empty `testName` makes `startsWith` vacuously true and `slice(0)` return the whole key, so the anchored regex is evaluated against the full key.
rationale: With `testName === ''`, `uncheckedKey.startsWith('')` is always true and the regex is tested against the entire key; a key that literally begins with a space and digits (or ` > `) would be deleted for an unrelated test. This existed before too, but the added guard gives a false impression of safety. Low severity / low likelihood, but an explicit empty-name early return would be clearer.

claim: `^ > ` alternative is unanchored at the end and still matches keys lacking a trailing counter, while `^ \d+$` requires an exact single-space-plus-digits remainder — the two branches are inconsistent.
rationale: For a hinted snapshot the remainder is ` > hint 1`; `^ > ` matches regardless of what follows, so a key such as `testName > something else entirely` (no counter) is also cleared. The non-hinted branch, by contrast, is strictly anchored. If the intent is to match only well-formed keys, the hint branch should be `^ > .* \d+$`. Low-to-moderate confidence that this matters in practice, but the asymmetry looks unintentional.

claim: The set's meaning is inverted (allowlist → denylist); every use site must have its predicate flipped or the VM/environment logic silently reverses.
rationale: Before, `DOM_ENVIRONMENTS.has(env)` was true only for jsdom/happy-dom (the environments with a VM upside). Now the set lists the environments *without* upside, so any call site that still reads `SET.has(env)` as "measure VM candidates" will now do exactly the opposite (measuring VM for node/edge-runtime and skipping it for jsdom/happy-dom). The hunk doesn't show the call sites, so I can't confirm they were updated to `!ENVIRONMENTS_WITHOUT_VM_UPSIDE.has(env)` — worth verifying; high impact if missed.

claim: An unset/empty `environment` (which defaults to 'node') is not a member of the new set, so the default project will now be treated as having a VM upside.
rationale: With the old allowlist, `undefined`/`''` fell outside jsdom/happy-dom and VM candidates were correctly skipped. With the denylist, `ENVIRONMENTS_WITHOUT_VM_UPSIDE.has(undefined)` is false, so the most common configuration (no `environment` specified → node) is now classified as VM-worthy. Unless the caller normalizes the value to 'node' before the lookup, this is a real behavior regression. Fairly confident this is a live edge case; depends on unseen normalization.

claim: Treating all unknown/custom environments as VM candidates makes the doctor run fail for custom environments that don't implement `setupVM`, instead of skipping them.
rationale: The added comment explicitly acknowledges "the run fails if they lack setupVM". A diagnostic/advisory command failing hard because a user's custom environment doesn't support VM mode is a poor failure mode; the candidate should either be probed (check for a `setupVM` export) or the measurement failure should be caught and reported as "not applicable" rather than aborting.

claim: Exact-string matching may miss equivalent environment specifiers such as a package-qualified name or path-based custom environment resolving to node.
rationale: Environments can be referenced by package name (e.g. `vitest-environment-node`) or configured per-file via `environmentMatchGlobs`/docblocks; a plain `Set.has()` on the root `environment` string won't catch those and will mis-classify them as VM-worthy. Low confidence that this matters in practice, but the denylist form makes mismatches fail open rather than closed.

claim: Browser mode now receives an empty `defines` object instead of `config.define`, silently dropping all user-configured defines for browser tests.
rationale: Previously `resolvedTestConfig.defines = config.define || {}` propagated Vite's `define` entries to the resolved test config for browser mode; the new branch assigns `{}`. Any consumer that reads `config.defines` at runtime (e.g. to stringify/serialize defines, or to expose them to the browser runner) will now see nothing. If the intent is that Vite itself already applies defines via transform in browser mode, this may be deliberate, but it is an observable behavior change for existing browser users and directly contradicts the adjacent comment "keep the original behaviour in the browser mode". Medium confidence that this is unintended; at minimum it deserves confirmation and a comment update.

claim: Reordering the conditions makes `isBrowserEnabled` shadow the `sharedServer` branch, so `_scriptDefines` is never populated when both are true.
rationale: Before, `sharedServer` took precedence and set both `defines` and `_scriptDefines` from the shared server even in browser mode. Now, when a shared server exists and browser mode is enabled, the first branch wins and `_scriptDefines` is left `undefined` (and the shared server's defines are discarded). Any downstream code that iterates or spreads `config._scriptDefines` without a null check will break, and defines shared across projects will be lost for browser projects. Worth verifying whether `_scriptDefines` consumers handle `undefined`.

claim: Synchronous `existsSync`/`mkdirSync` are used inside an otherwise async method, blocking the event loop, and the `existsSync` guard is redundant with `recursive: true`.
rationale: `mkdirSync(path, { recursive: true })` is already a no-op when the directory exists, so the `existsSync` guard adds nothing except a TOCTOU race window. Since this is an `async` method that already awaits `writeFile`, `await mkdir(this.rootCache, { recursive: true })` would avoid blocking the main thread. Confident about the redundancy; the blocking concern is a real but modest perf issue.

claim: Only `this.rootCache` is created, but `this.metadataFilePath` may live in a nested subdirectory, in which case `writeFile` will still fail with ENOENT.
rationale: The directory creation assumes `metadataFilePath` is a direct child of `rootCache`. If the metadata path is nested deeper (or derived differently), the mkdir won't create the needed parent and the write silently fails through the catch. Safer to `mkdir(dirname(this.metadataFilePath), { recursive: true })`. I cannot see the field definitions in this hunk, so this is a suspicion rather than a confirmed bug.

claim: Non-atomic write of the metadata file can leave a truncated/corrupt file that a concurrent or subsequent reader interprets as "no metadata".
rationale: `writeFile` truncates then writes; if the process is killed mid-write, or two Vitest instances share the same cache root, a reader gets partial JSON. The reader swallows the parse error (`catch {}`), so the failure mode is a silent full cache invalidation. Writing to a temp file and `rename`-ing would make it atomic. Moderate confidence this matters in practice when multiple projects share one cache dir.

claim: Completely swallowing write failures means the cache-integrity check can never converge: every subsequent run will see a missing/stale lockfile hash and nuke the cache.
rationale: The comment frames this as best-effort, which is reasonable for not aborting the run, but a persistent failure (e.g. read-only FS, permission error) degrades silently into "cache is always cold" with only a debug-level message. Consider a one-time warn, or distinguishing EACCES/EROFS from transient errors. Low-to-moderate confidence this rises above intentional design.

claim: `debugFs?.(`...${error}`)` is the only error surface and stringifying the error loses the stack trace.
rationale: `${error}` yields only `Error: message` with no stack, making diagnosis hard for the one place this code reports problems; if `debugFs` is undefined the failure is entirely invisible. Passing the error object (or `error.stack`) would retain context. Minor but directly affects debuggability of a silently-failing path.

claim: New code depends on `existsSync`, `mkdirSync`, and `writeFile` being imported; if any are not already in scope the change will not compile.
rationale: The hunk adds three fs API usages but shows no import changes. The file previously did async reads, so `writeFile` from `node:fs/promises` and the sync helpers from `node:fs` may or may not already be imported. Flagging for verification only — cannot confirm from the shown context.

claim: When `root` normalizes to the filesystem root ("/"), the returned relative dist dir loses its leading separator, unlike every other root value.
rationale: `normalizedRoot.length` is used for the slice instead of `rootPrefix.length`, deliberately preserving the leading '/' (root '/a' + dist '/a/dist' -> '/dist'). But for normalizedRoot === '/', length is 1 and the slice removes the separator, yielding 'dist' instead of '/dist'. This inconsistency will surprise any caller that concatenates or path-joins the result. High confidence this is an inconsistency; impact depends on the (not-shown) call site.

claim: `startsWith` is case- and drive-letter-sensitive, so a root that actually contains distDir can silently return "" on Windows or case-insensitive macOS volumes.
rationale: Paths like 'C:/proj' vs 'c:/proj', or differing case on a case-insensitive APFS/HFS+ volume, are the same directory but fail the exact string prefix test, producing the 'not contained' sentinel. Moderate confidence this matters in practice for Vitest's Windows support.

claim: The empty-string return value conflates three distinct cases: distDir outside root, root === distDir, and a failed prefix match.
rationale: When `root` equals `distDir`, `rootPrefix` gains a trailing slash so `startsWith` is false and '' is returned, the same as the genuinely-outside-root case. Callers cannot distinguish 'no relative path' from 'dist dir is the root itself'. Returning null/undefined for the not-contained case would be unambiguous. Medium confidence this causes a real bug without seeing the consumer.

claim: The trailing-slash regex, the `${normalizedRoot}/` prefix, and the `=== '/'` check all assume `normalize` emits POSIX separators.
rationale: If `normalize` is Node's `path.normalize` rather than pathe's, on Windows it emits backslashes and none of this logic works (regex won't strip 'C:\\', prefix mixes separators, startsWith fails). Low-to-medium confidence since Vitest usually imports from pathe, but the import is outside the shown hunk and worth verifying.

claim: The new `mockPrototype !== parent` guard only prevents a *direct* self-cycle; an indirect cycle (where `parent`'s own prototype chain already contains `mockPrototype`) still throws `TypeError: Cyclic __proto__ value`.
rationale: `Object.setPrototypeOf` rejects any assignment that would create a cycle, not just `setPrototypeOf(o, o)`. If an implementation is a subclass whose `prototype` chain passes through `mockPrototype` (realistic when a mock is used as a base class, or when a mocked class's prototype was previously reparented onto this mock), `mockPrototype !== parent` is true and `Object.getPrototypeOf(mockPrototype) !== parent` is true, so the code still calls `setPrototypeOf` and throws. A chain walk (`let p = parent; while (p) { if (p === mockPrototype) return; p = Object.getPrototypeOf(p) }`) or a try/catch would cover the general case. Moderate confidence this is reachable in practice; high confidence the guard is incomplete in principle.

claim: When `mockPrototype === parent`, the function now silently leaves the previous prototype in place instead of reverting the chain, so a stale parent from an earlier implementation can leak.
rationale: The comment directly above states the invariant that an implementation without a usable prototype reverts the chain to `Object.prototype`. With the new guard, the self-referential case takes the early-skip path and keeps whatever parent a *previous* `mockImplementation` installed, rather than resetting to `Object.prototype`. If the goal is only to avoid the TypeError, the safer behavior is likely `Object.setPrototypeOf(mockPrototype, Object.prototype)` in that branch. Medium confidence — depends on whether the self-referential case is ever reached after a prior non-trivial implementation.

claim: `parent` is still not validated as object-or-null, so a non-object `.prototype` (e.g. `fn.prototype = 42`) reaches `Object.setPrototypeOf` and throws a `TypeError`.
rationale: `(implementation as Constructable | undefined)?.prototype ?? Object.prototype` only defends against `null`/`undefined`. A function whose `prototype` has been assigned a primitive yields a primitive `parent`; `Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, 42)` throws TypeError. Pre-existing rather than introduced by this hunk, but since the change is specifically hardening this call site it is worth covering here. Low-to-medium confidence that it matters in practice.

claim: New import of `toRollupError` from `./environments/fetchModule` may introduce a circular import / pull server-only code into `ast-collect.ts`.
rationale: `ast-collect.ts` is a fairly low-level collection helper, while `environments/fetchModule` is a Vite/module-runner server concern that typically imports other node-side modules (project/vite server types, error helpers). If that chain imports back into the collector or into modules that import `ast-collect`, the ESM cycle can yield `toRollupError` being `undefined` at call time (a TypeError only at runtime, not build time). Even without a cycle, this adds module-load side effects/heavier deps to a file that is imported during test collection. Worth verifying the dependency direction and, if in doubt, moving `toRollupError` into a leaf util module. Low-to-moderate confidence since I can only see the import line, not the module graph.

claim: Verify `toRollupError` is actually exported from `./environments/fetchModule` and is actually used in this file.
rationale: The hunk only shows the added import; if the usage lives in another (unshown) hunk this is fine, but if the call site was removed/renamed during the change this leaves an unused import that still forces evaluation of `fetchModule` at load time. Also, if `toRollupError` is only a type-level helper or is exported under a different name, this would be a build error. Low confidence — cannot verify from the shown context alone.

claim: The new `MarkOptions.kind` is typed as the full `BrowserTraceEntryKind` union, allowing callers to emit `'action'`, `'expect'`, or `'lifecycle'` entries through the public mark API
rationale: `'action'`, `'expect'` and `'lifecycle'` look like kinds the runtime itself produces for locator actions, assertions and test lifecycle boundaries. Exposing them on a user-facing `mark()` option lets user code inject entries that the trace viewer (and any logic that pairs lifecycle start/end entries) treats as engine-generated, which can corrupt the rendered trace. The documented default `'mark'` suggests a marker-only subset was intended. Medium confidence — depends on how the consumer of `kind` interprets the values, which is not visible in this hunk.

claim: `stack?: string` is an untyped free-form string with no documented format or defined failure behavior when it cannot be parsed
rationale: Stack parsing is environment-dependent (V8 vs Firefox/Safari formats). Accepting an arbitrary string means a wrapper library passing a non-V8 or truncated stack will silently produce a wrong or missing marker location, or potentially throw during parsing. Worth confirming the consumer falls back to a captured stack rather than emitting a bogus file/line. Low-to-medium confidence since the parsing code is not in this hunk.

claim: `MarkOptions` is a very generic name newly added to the public `vitest/browser` type surface
rationale: As a newly exported public symbol, a generic name like `MarkOptions` can collide with declarations from other packages in consumers' ambient/merged type space and is ambiguous next to the more specific sibling `BrowserTraceEntryKind`. `BrowserMarkOptions` would be consistent and reduce collision risk. This affects the published API shape, though practical impact is low.

claim: The newly added block mutates global `process.exitCode` from inside a library/Node-API method, a surprising side effect for programmatic callers.
rationale: `Vitest#collect`-style APIs are used programmatically (editor integrations, the public Node API, tests of Vitest itself). Setting `process.exitCode = 1` here makes the *host* process exit non-zero even though the caller may have handled the failed modules itself, and there is no code path that ever resets it back to 0 (e.g. on a subsequent successful watch-mode collection). Normally exit-code decisions belong to the CLI entry point, which already inspects the returned state. Moderately confident this is a behavior change worth a second look.

claim: Failures are signalled only through `process.exitCode`; the returned object still reports `unhandledErrors: []`, so programmatic callers get no indication of the failure.
rationale: If static parsing produced failed tasks (e.g. a syntax/collection error recorded on the module task), the return value is indistinguishable from a fully successful collection. Any caller that checks `unhandledErrors` (or just the returned `testModules`) to decide success will silently treat this as a pass. Either the errors should be surfaced in the return value, or the exit-code mutation should be moved to the caller that can inspect `testModules`.

claim: Only the `staticParse` branch sets `process.exitCode`; the `collectTests` fallback branch does not, creating inconsistent exit-code behavior between the two collection modes.
rationale: Users toggling `staticParse` (or hitting the fallback path) will get a zero exit code for the same failing collection. If setting the exit code is the desired contract for this method, it should be applied uniformly after both branches. Fairly confident this asymmetry is unintended, unless `collectTests` already sets it internally — worth verifying.

claim: `hasFailed` must be imported in this module; verify the import exists and that it accepts a `Task[]` (not a suite/file tree) in the current runner-utils signature.
rationale: The diff only shows the usage, not an import addition. If `hasFailed` is not already imported in `core.ts`, this is a compile error. Additionally, `hasFailed` in @vitest/runner/utils traverses suite `tasks` recursively; passing the top-level module tasks is likely correct, but a static-parse module whose *own* `result` was never set while a child task carries the error state (or vice versa) could be missed. Low-to-medium confidence; needs a quick check of the import list and of how parse errors are recorded on the task.

claim: `@experimental` is replaced by `@default true` for `staticParse`, asserting static parsing is on by default — this should be verified against actual config resolution, and it silently promotes an experimental flag to stable API.
rationale: `staticParse?: boolean` is optional, so the documented default only holds if the resolver actually falls back to `true` (e.g. `staticParse ?? true`). If resolution still defaults to `false`/undefined, the doc is wrong and callers will assume static collection when it isn't happening. Dropping `@experimental` is also a stability commitment: if the flag can still change or be removed, that signal is lost for users and for tooling that keys on the tag. Moderate confidence — I cannot see the resolution code from this hunk.

claim: `@default os.availableParallelism()` for `staticParseConcurrency` may not match the real default, and `os.availableParallelism()` is unavailable on Node < 18.14/19.4.
rationale: Two concerns. (1) Accuracy: the documented default must match the resolver; implementations often use `os.cpus().length`, `availableParallelism() - 1`, or a fixed cap, which would make this misleading for anyone tuning concurrency. (2) Portability: `os.availableParallelism` only exists from Node 18.14/19.4 onward, so if the implementation calls it without a fallback it throws on older supported Node versions, and the doc now advertises that exact call. Also worth confirming the resolver guards against `0`/negative/non-integer user values, since `0` concurrency could stall parsing. Medium confidence — only the JSDoc is visible here.

claim: `ctx.clearCache()` may not exist on the Vitest instance, causing a runtime `TypeError: ctx.clearCache is not a function` when `--clearCache` is passed.
rationale: The diff only shows the call site being renamed from `experimental_clearCache` to `clearCache`. If the corresponding method on the `Vitest` class (and its public type declarations / `.d.ts`) was not renamed or aliased in the same change, this call resolves to `undefined` and throws at runtime on the exact CLI path it is meant to serve. Worth confirming the class-side rename landed; I cannot see the class definition in this hunk, so confidence is moderate.

claim: Dropping the `experimental_` prefix is a public API break for external callers that still invoke `experimental_clearCache()`.
rationale: `experimental_clearCache` was an exported/public method on the Vitest node API, not internal-only. If the old name was removed rather than kept as a deprecated alias, any programmatic consumer calling it breaks without a deprecation cycle. Also, promoting an experimental API to stable implies the behavior/signature is now committed to; that should be intentional and documented. Confidence moderate — the removal itself is outside this hunk.

claim: Potential name collision: `clearCache` is also the name of the config flag (`ctx.config.clearCache`) and may shadow or conflict with an existing differently-behaving method of the same name.
rationale: Renaming to a generic `clearCache` increases the chance of colliding with a pre-existing member (e.g. an internal cache-clearing helper used during watch-mode reruns) that has different semantics. If such a member exists, the rename silently overrides it and `--clearCache` would perform the wrong operation. Low-to-moderate confidence; needs a grep of the Vitest class for an existing `clearCache` member.

claim: The call was renamed to `this.parseSpecifications(...)`, but it's not shown that a method with that name exists on `Vitest`. If only `experimental_parseSpecifications` is declared (and the rename wasn't applied to the method declaration in the same commit), this path throws `TypeError: this.parseSpecifications is not a function` at runtime whenever `options.staticParse` is set.
rationale: The hunk only touches the call site; the declaration is not visible here. Renaming a call without the corresponding declaration is a common partial-rename mistake, and this particular branch is only reached with `staticParse`, so it may not be covered by default test runs. Medium confidence — needs a grep for `parseSpecifications` across the package.

claim: Dropping the `experimental_` prefix changes a public API surface of the `Vitest` class. Any external caller (or other internal call sites / re-exports / type declarations) still using `experimental_parseSpecifications` will break unless a deprecated alias is kept.
rationale: The `experimental_` prefix is Vitest's convention for opt-in unstable APIs, and graduating one is a documented breaking change. If no back-compat alias is added, consumers on the old name break silently at runtime. Reasonably confident this is worth checking, though it may be intentional for a major release.

claim: Deferring `utils.getMessage(...)` into the failure branch changes when message serialization runs, so any side effect or throw during message/`objDisplay` formatting of `args` no longer happens on the passing path.
rationale: Chai's `getMessage` stringifies the expected value (`args`) via `objDisplay`/inspection. Previously that ran on every assertion, including passing ones; now it only runs when the assertion fails. In practice this is almost certainly the intent (avoid formatting cost on the hot passing path) and an improvement, but it is a real behavior change: an argument whose `toString`/`inspect`/getters throw or mutate state would previously have surfaced on passing assertions and now will not. Low confidence that this matters to any real caller, but flagging since it is the only semantic delta in the hunk. Note also that `spyName` (`spy.getMockName()`) is still computed eagerly, so the optimization is only partial, and the sibling assertions such as `toHaveBeenCalledExactlyOnceWith` below retain the eager pattern, leaving the codebase inconsistent.

claim: The new `prewarmModules: false` property is added inside an object written with a type assertion (`<Environment>{...}`), which does not apply excess-property checking. If `prewarmModules` is not actually declared on the `Environment` interface (or is spelled differently there, e.g. `prewarm`/`preloadModules`), TypeScript will silently accept it and the flag will be a no-op at runtime.
rationale: Type assertions on object literals only require comparability, so extra/misspelled keys compile cleanly. Worth verifying the property exists on the `Environment` type (and is read by the runner) — medium confidence, since I cannot see the type definition in this hunk.

claim: Disabling prewarming for the `node` environment is a behavior change for the default environment: every project that does not explicitly set `environment` now loses module prewarming, which could regress startup/run time or change module-instantiation ordering observed by existing tests.
rationale: `node` is Vitest's default environment, so this opt-out applies to the vast majority of users rather than a niche env. If the intent was only to skip prewarming in the VM path (`setupVM`), a per-environment static flag applies to both `setup()` and `setupVM()`. Low-to-medium confidence that this is unintended, but it is a broad, silent behavior change worth confirming.

claim: Only the node environment declares `prewarmModules`; other built-in environments (jsdom, happy-dom, edge-runtime) presumably still rely on an implicit default. If the consuming code reads `env.prewarmModules` without a defined default (e.g. `if (env.prewarmModules)` vs `!== false`), the undefined value in the other environments may be coerced to the opposite of the intended default.
rationale: Introducing an optional tri-state (true/false/undefined) flag is easy to mishandle at the call site; the default semantics for the environments that omit it should be explicit. Low confidence without seeing the consumer, but a plausible source of inconsistency.

claim: The `reports` import from `istanbul-reports` is deleted without any replacement import (no `@vitest/istanbul-reports` line is added), so any remaining `reports.create(...)` call in this file will be an unresolved reference / TS compile error.
rationale: Every other istanbul package in the hunk gets a `@vitest/*` replacement, but `istanbul-reports` is simply dropped. `istanbul-lib-report` (the report context builder) is replaced and is normally paired with `istanbul-reports` for `reports.create('html')`. Unless a later hunk removes all report creation or re-exports `reports` from `@vitest/istanbul-lib-report`, this breaks report generation. I can't see the rest of the file, so medium confidence — worth verifying no `reports.` usage remains.

claim: `istanbulDefaults` from `@istanbuljs/schema` is removed with no replacement; remaining uses (e.g. default instrumenter/coverage options) would become undefined references.
rationale: Same concern as the `reports` removal: the import is dropped but nothing in this hunk supplies the defaults. `istanbulDefaults` is typically used for `createInstrumenter` options or default excludes in this provider. If those usages remain elsewhere in the file this is a hard break; if the fork inlines the defaults, it's fine. Medium confidence, flagged for verification.

claim: Switching `import libCoverage from 'istanbul-lib-coverage'` to `import * as libCoverage from '@vitest/istanbul-lib-coverage'` changes interop shape; if the new package still ships CJS with `module.exports = {...}`, `libCoverage.createCoverageMap` may resolve to `undefined` (members would live under `libCoverage.default`).
rationale: Default-import vs namespace-import over CJS behaves differently depending on `esModuleInterop`/`allowSyntheticDefaultImports` and whether Node's cjs-module-lexer detects the named exports. Since the package is presumably an ESM fork with real named exports this is likely intentional, but it is the classic failure mode for this migration. Low-to-medium confidence; the same concern applies to `libReport` (line 12) and `libSourceMaps` (line 13) but I report it once here.

claim: Type-only imports now come from `@vitest/istanbul-lib-coverage` / `@vitest/istanbul-lib-instrument` while other code (and `vitest/node`'s `CoverageProvider` surface) may still reference the original `istanbul-lib-coverage` types, yielding two nominally distinct `CoverageMap`/`Instrumenter` declarations.

claim: Copying the request's `Content-Type` onto the rebuilt `Response` changes the `type` of blobs returned by `blob()` (and the effective media type for other representations) from `''` to the original media type, a silent behavior change for existing callers.

This is arguably more correct, but it is an observable change not limited to the `formData()` case the comment describes. Confidence: high that the behavior changes, medium that it matters to callers.

claim: With the content type now preserved, `formData()` rebuilt from a `text`-cached body can silently produce corrupted/incorrect parts instead of failing fast.
rationale: When the cached key is `text`, the original bytes were already decoded to a JS string; re-encoding that string as the body of a multipart/form-data response is lossy for binary file parts (and for any non-UTF-8 payload). Before this change such a call threw immediately because no content type was present; now it will parse and hand back plausible-looking but potentially corrupted `File` contents. Same concern applies when the cached key is `json`, where `JSON.stringify` produces bytes that differ from the original body while the original `Content-Type` is still advertised. Confidence: medium-high.

claim: The truthiness check on `contentType` conflates an absent header with an empty-string header value.
rationale: `raw.headers.get('content-type')` returns `null` when absent but `''` if the header is present and empty; both fall into the `undefined` branch. Functionally close to harmless, but an explicit `!== null` check would be more precise, and an empty string would otherwise be an invalid header value anyway. Low confidence that this has practical impact.

claim: Filtering out q === 0 entries discards the negation information, so an explicitly rejected type can still be served via a surviving wildcard entry.
rationale: RFC 9110 12.5.1 uses q=0 not just to demote an entry but to exclude that media range. With `Accept: */*, text/html;q=0` the `text/html;q=0` entry is removed by the filter, leaving only `*/*`, which matchType will match against a supported `text/html`, returning exactly the type the client rejected. Correct handling requires keeping zero-q entries as an exclusion list checked against each candidate in `supports`, not filtering them away. Fairly confident this is a real gap, assuming matchType treats wildcards as matching (which getSpecificity implies).

claim: `accept.q > 0` silently discards entries whose q is NaN or undefined, potentially emptying the whole candidate list.
rationale: The declared type is `q: number`, but header parsers commonly yield NaN for malformed values like `q=abc`, and an entry with no q parameter may be left undefined depending on the parser. Both `NaN > 0` and `undefined > 0` are false, so such entries are dropped and the function falls through to defaultSupport, whereas previously they were still considered for matching. A defensive form such as `(accept.q ?? 1) > 0` or `!(accept.q <= 0)` would preserve prior behavior. Medium confidence; depends on the parser feeding this function.

claim: When every accept entry has q=0, the loop now matches nothing and the function returns defaultSupport, serving content the client explicitly declared unacceptable.
rationale: `Accept: */*;q=0` previously matched and returned a supported type; after this change sortedAccepts is empty and control falls through to the default return. Returning the default contradicts the stated intent that zero-q entries must never match - a 406 would arguably be required. Even if defaulting is the deliberate contract of this helper, callers relying on the previous match result see a silent behavior change worth covering in tests. Moderate confidence this is an unintended edge case.

claim: `pipeline()` destroys the writable on error, which can break existing error-handling in the caller that still writes to / ends the response stream
rationale: The old implementation only rejected on a read error and left `writer` untouched (never ended, never destroyed), so callers of `streamToNodeStream` could still `responseStream.write(...)`/`.end()` in a catch block to emit an error body. `stream/promises.pipeline` destroys both source and destination when either side errors, so any subsequent `write`/`end` on the Lambda response stream will throw `ERR_STREAM_DESTROYED` or emit an unhandled 'error'. Fairly confident this is a real behavior change; worth checking the catch block in `streamHandle`.

claim: The async generator never cancels/releases the web `ReadableStreamDefaultReader` when the pipeline is torn down early
rationale: When the destination errors or is destroyed, `pipeline` calls `.return()` on the generator, which resumes at the `yield`. Without a `try { ... } finally { reader.cancel() }` (or `releaseLock()`), the underlying web stream is left un-cancelled and its resources/body are leaked, and the upstream producer is never told to stop. The previous code had the same gap, but the new generator form makes early termination much more likely, so adding the finally is worthwhile. Medium confidence on impact, high confidence on the missing cleanup.

rationale: `NodeJS.WritableStream` only guarantees `write`/`end`/`on`, whereas the old code only ever needed `write`/`end`. `stream/promises.pipeline` duck-types its destination (requires `on`, `once`, `emit`, `destroy`/`_writableState` handling via `isNodeStream`/`Writable.toWeb` paths) and throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` for objects that don't qualify. AWS's `awslambda.HttpResponseStream.from(...)` normally returns a real Writable so this probably works, but the declared parameter type no longer matches what the implementation requires — consider narrowing it to `NodeJS.WritableStream & Writable`/`Writable`. Moderate confidence.

claim: Verify `pipeline` is imported from `node:stream/promises`, not `node:stream`
rationale: The new body returns `pipeline(...)` directly as a `Promise<void>`. The callback-based `stream.pipeline` returns the destination stream and requires a callback, so an import from `node:stream` would both fail to typecheck and silently never resolve/report errors. The import line isn't in this hunk, so I can't confirm it; flagging for verification.

If only `set` accepts `PropertyKey`, callers can write `c.set(mySymbol, v)` but `c.get(mySymbol)` will fail to type-check (and `c.get('Symbol(...)')` won't find it in the Map). Unless `get`, the `Get`/`Set` interface declarations, and `ContextVariableMap` handling are updated in the same change, this is an incomplete/asymmetric widening. Fairly confident this is worth verifying; I can't see the `get` declaration in this hunk.

claim: Non-string keys stored in `#var` break the `c.var` getter, which typically does `Object.fromEntries(this.#var)`: numeric keys are coerced to strings (so `1` and `'1'` collide in the object but not in the Map) and symbol keys become non-enumerable-ish/invisible to spread and JSON.

Confidence is moderate-to-high given Hono's `var` getter implementation, but it depends on code outside this hunk.

Any downstream type that does `keyof E['Variables']`, `Extract<keyof V, string>`, or template-literal key manipulation will now see `string | number | symbol` instead of `string`, which can silently break key-constrained helper types or make previously-rejected keys allowed. Medium confidence that something downstream depends on the string-only index signature; worth checking type tests.

rationale: The arrow function is typed by the `Set<...>` type, so the declared parameter type here is only checked for assignability (contravariance permits widening) and does not widen the call signature seen by consumers. If the `Set` type definition wasn't updated in the same commit, this change has no observable effect on callers while still allowing non-string keys into `#var` from internal call sites. Low-to-medium confidence since the `Set` type isn't shown.

Worth verifying against multi-param routes where only the first key can be overridden by `params`. Medium confidence this is a latent hazard rather than an immediate bug.

RFC 9110 allows ETag/If-None-Match on error and redirect responses, so this is a real behavior change for existing callers; confidence moderate-high that it is intentional but worth confirming it is documented/tested.

This may be the intent of the change, but it is a silent breaking change and deserves a documented note or an opt-out option.

If the guard's goal is to limit ETag generation to full cacheable representations, 206 should be excluded explicitly. Confidence moderate — depends on whether range handling exists elsewhere in the stack.

claim: The method comparison is exact-case and will fall through (skipping ETag handling entirely) for a lowercase or mixed-case method string.
rationale: Hono normally surfaces the raw method from the incoming request, which is uppercase for conformant clients, but some runtimes/adapters or manually constructed `Request` objects can carry e.g. `get`. Using `c.req.method.toUpperCase()` would make the guard robust. Low confidence this occurs in practice, but the failure mode is silent.

claim: Adding `preventAbort: true` silently swallows source-stream errors into the response: the destination WritableStream is no longer errored/aborted when `body` errors mid-stream, so a truncated response can be finalized as if it completed successfully.
rationale: Previously, if `body` errored, `pipeTo` aborted `this.writable`, which normally propagates the failure to the underlying response/socket so the client sees a broken/aborted transfer rather than a valid-looking truncated body. With `preventAbort`, the destination is left open and healthy; the rejection still surfaces from `pipe()`, but whether the caller turns that into an abort of the response is now entirely up to the caller. If callers just log or ignore the rejection (common for streaming handlers), clients will receive silently truncated data. Reasonably confident this is a real semantic change worth an explicit decision/comment; it may be intentional if the goal is to keep writing after a failed pipe.

claim: `this.writable.getWriter()` inside `finally` can throw and mask the original `pipeTo` rejection.
rationale: If the writable is still locked (e.g. a pathological/custom stream implementation, or an implementation where the lock release is not yet observable) or otherwise unusable, `getWriter()` throws a TypeError from the `finally` block, which replaces the real pipe error and makes debugging much harder. Wrapping the reacquire in its own try/catch, or reacquiring only when the lock is actually free, would preserve the original error. Moderate confidence — in a spec-compliant implementation pipeTo releases the lock before settling, so this is mainly defensive.

claim: After a failed pipe the newly acquired writer may be attached to an already-errored writable, so subsequent `write`/`close` calls will reject and can become unhandled rejections.
rationale: `getWriter()` succeeds on an errored (but unlocked) stream; the failure only appears on the next `write()`/`close()`/`ready`. With `preventAbort` the destination survives source errors, but a destination-side error (the other failure mode of `pipeTo`) still leaves `this.writable` errored. Re-assigning `this.writer` unconditionally means later `write()` calls in this class (which are often not awaited/caught) will produce rejected promises. Consider tracking an `aborted`/`closed` flag and skipping the reacquire when the stream is errored. Medium confidence.

claim: The failure path does not notify `abortSubscribers` or mark the stream as aborted.
rationale: The class maintains `abortSubscribers`/`onAbort`, presumably fired when the stream is torn down. Now that `pipe()` deliberately keeps the destination alive on error, a failed pipe leaves the object in a 'still writable' state with no abort notification, so consumers relying on `onAbort` for cleanup never run. Low-to-medium confidence since I can't see the rest of the class, but worth checking against how `abort()`/`close()` handle this.

claim: The newly added `relaxedCookieNameRegEx` is not wired into any code in this hunk; if `parse()` still tests names with `validCookieNameRegEx`, the fix is a no-op and the constant is dead code (which also trips `noUnusedLocals`/lint in many TS setups).
