rationale: Verified the intended set matches the comment (33-126 minus 34, 59, 61, 92), so behavior today is correct; the concern is fragility/readability of the escaping, not current output. Escaping as `>-\[` would be safer. Confidence: high on the escaping fact, low on it causing a bug today.

claim: Parsing and serialization now use different name grammars, so a cookie read from the request (e.g. `paraglide:lang`) can no longer be re-emitted through `setCookie`/`serialize` without throwing — a behavior change for middleware that copies or refreshes incoming cookies.
rationale: This asymmetry is deliberate per the added comments, but callers that round-trip parsed names into `setCookie` will start hitting the strict-regex validation error for names that previously were simply dropped at parse time. Worth confirming the error is thrown (not silently swallowed) and documented. Medium confidence, since the serialize path is outside this hunk.

claim: `buildData[0][4] && getServerSnapshot` is now evaluated on every render instead of being latched once in `useState`, so the server-snapshot branch is no longer sticky/one-shot and `getServerSnapshot()` may be re-invoked on every render.
rationale: Previously the decision was frozen at mount (`const [serverSnapshotIsUsed] = useState(...)`) and the client snapshot was adopted in the effect. Now, if `buildData[0][4]` (the SSR/hydration flag) stays truthy for the lifetime of the node, `snapshot` will be the *server* snapshot forever and the component will never reflect store updates (the `update()` bump re-renders but re-reads the server snapshot again). Conversely, if the flag flips mid-lifecycle the returned value changes without any state transition. Also, `getServerSnapshot` is now called on each render rather than once, which is a behavior change for non-trivial implementations. I'm not certain of the exact semantics of `buildData[0][4]`, but the loss of the latched state is a real semantic change worth verifying.

claim: `useRef<() => void>(null)` passes `null` for a ref typed as non-nullable `() => void`; the type argument should include `null` (`useRef<(() => void) | null>(null)`).
rationale: With hono/jsx's `useRef<T>(initialValue: T): RefObject<T>` signature this is a type error (or, if it compiles via an overload, `unsubscribeRef.current` is typed as non-nullable while actually being `null` until the first effect flush — the `?.()` calls show the author knows it can be null). Unsafe typing rather than a runtime bug, but it can hide a real null deref if someone later drops the optional chaining.

claim: The subscription callback now unconditionally bumps a version counter instead of comparing snapshots, so every store notification forces a re-render even when `getSnapshot()` returns the same value.
rationale: The old `setState(getSnapshot())` bailed out when the snapshot was `Object.is`-equal. `setVersion(v => v + 1)` always changes state, so a store that notifies broadly (a common pattern, e.g. a single global emitter with per-selector snapshots) will now re-render every subscriber on every notification. Correctness is preserved but this is a noticeable perf/behavior regression; a `Object.is(latestSnapshot.current[0], latestSnapshot.current[1]())` guard inside `update` would restore the bail-out.

claim: Changing the effect deps from `[]` to `[subscribe]` introduces a render-loop risk when callers pass an inline `subscribe` together with a `getSnapshot` that returns a fresh value each call.
rationale: With `[subscribe]` deps and an inline arrow `subscribe`, the effect re-runs after every render; if `getSnapshot()` is not referentially stable (returns a new object/array), `!Object.is(snapshot, getSnapshot())` is always true, so `update()` fires, which re-renders, which re-runs the effect — an infinite loop. The previous `[]` deps made this impossible. React guards against this with a dev-time warning; here there is none. Callers that were previously (accidentally) fine will now spin.

claim: `unsubscribeRef.current?.()` at the top of the effect replaces a returned cleanup, so unsubscription is no longer tied to the effect lifecycle; if the second (`[]`) effect's cleanup is not guaranteed to run on unmount in all paths, the subscription leaks.
rationale: The subscription teardown now depends entirely on a separate `useEffect(..., [])` cleanup. Any code path that tears down the component without flushing that effect's cleanup (e.g. unmount before the effects for that commit are flushed, or error during render/effect after `subscribe` returned) leaves the store subscribed with a callback holding the dead component's `setVersion`. The old code's returned cleanup was tied to the same effect that created the subscription. Worth confirming hono/jsx always runs `[]`-effect cleanups on unmount even when the component unmounts in the same pass it mounted.

claim: `scopes` is declared as a required property (`string[] | null`) inside the optional `jwt` object, but API Gateway omits `scopes` entirely for non-OAuth JWTs
rationale: In the real HTTP API v2 payload, `authorizer.jwt` frequently contains only `claims`; `scopes` is absent rather than `null`. Declaring it required means anyone constructing this type (tests, mocks, adapters) must supply `scopes: null`, and consumers reading `ctx.authorizer.jwt.scopes` will be told it is always present when at runtime it can be `undefined`. `scopes?: string[]` (matching @types/aws-lambda's `APIGatewayEventRequestContextJWTAuthorizer`) would be safer. Moderately confident this is a mismatch with the actual event shape.

claim: `jwt`, `lambda` and the existing `iam` are all independently optional instead of a discriminated union, so mutually exclusive shapes type-check
rationale: An API Gateway authorizer context carries exactly one of `jwt`, `lambda`, or `iam`. With three optional members, code like `ctx.authorizer.jwt.claims` is only guarded by an optional-chain hint, and a consumer can write `if (ctx.authorizer.lambda) ... ctx.authorizer.jwt` without any compile error, producing `undefined` at runtime. A union (`{ jwt: ... } | { lambda: ... } | { iam: ... }`) would force correct narrowing. Confident this weakens the safety the type is meant to provide, though it may be a deliberate simplification.

claim: `lambda?: Record<string, unknown> | null` combines optional, nullable and `unknown` values, forcing unsafe casts at every read site and giving two distinct representations of "absent"
rationale: A Lambda REQUEST authorizer's `context` can only contain string/number/boolean values (API Gateway stringifies them), so `Record<string, string | number | boolean>` would be both accurate and usable. With `unknown`, callers doing `ctx.authorizer.lambda?.userId` and passing it to a string parameter need an `as string` cast, which hides shape bugs. Additionally the doc comment says it is `null` when there is no context, yet the property is also optional, so callers must handle both `undefined` and `null`. Medium confidence this will bite consumers.

claim: `jwt`/`lambda` are added to the shared `Authorizer` interface, which appears to back the v1 (REST) request context as well as v2
rationale: The members visible just above (`iam.cognitoIdentity`, `principalOrgId`, `userArn`, `userId`) are the REST/IAM shape, and `ApiGatewayRequestContextV2` is declared immediately after, suggesting this one interface is reused by both context types. `jwt` and `lambda` only exist in the HTTP API v2 payload format, so attaching them here advertises fields that will always be `undefined` on v1 events and lets v1 handlers branch on them. Worth confirming whether a separate `AuthorizerV2` is needed; I cannot see the usage sites in this hunk, so this is a suspicion rather than a certainty.

claim: The new cache-hit fast path skips the Content-Type handling done by bufferToFormData(arrayBuffer, headers.get('Content-Type') || ''), so parseBody can now succeed (or return different data) for requests whose Content-Type the slow path would have rejected.
rationale: Previously every call went through bufferToFormData with the request's Content-Type, which branches on multipart vs urlencoded and throws for unsupported/malformed types. With a pre-populated bodyCache.formData (set by a prior c.req.formData() call or middleware) that validation is bypassed. Medium confidence this is an intended trade-off, but it is a visible behavior change for existing callers.

claim: A cached bodyCache.formData that is a rejecting promise is awaited here with no try/catch, so parseBody now re-throws that cached parse error, and awaiting a shared promise can leave an unhandled rejection path.
rationale: bodyCache.formData may hold an in-flight Promise<FormData> stored by HonoRequest.formData() or by the tail of this same function; if parsing fails it rejects. Before this change parseBody produced its own error from arrayBuffer()/bufferToFormData. Moderate confidence; depends on how the cache is populated elsewhere.

claim: The cast `await (request.bodyCache.formData as FormData | Promise<FormData>)` is an unchecked assertion; if bodyCache.formData holds anything other than a FormData/Promise<FormData> (e.g. a rejected placeholder or a non-FormData value set by user code), convertFormDataToBodyData will receive an unexpected shape instead of failing loudly.
rationale: The truthiness check plus the cast performs no runtime validation. Low-to-medium confidence that this matters in practice, but the assertion hides a potential type mismatch that the previous code path could not hit.

claim: On a cache hit the converted BodyData is not memoized and aliases values (e.g. File entries) from the shared cached FormData, so repeated parseBody calls re-do the conversion and callers can observe/mutate objects shared with c.req.formData().
rationale: Minor efficiency and aliasing concern introduced by reusing the cached FormData instead of re-parsing a fresh buffer; low confidence this is problematic, but worth a second look if callers mutate the returned body data.

claim: `createNullObject()` must return a *fresh* object on every call; if it is memoized/returns a shared singleton, every `Node` instance would share the same `#children` map.
rationale: This is a class field initializer, so it runs once per instance. `Object.create(null)` unconditionally allocates a new object; a helper named `createNullObject` could plausibly be implemented as a cached constant (e.g. `const NULL_OBJ = Object.create(null); export const createNullObject = () => NULL_OBJ`) or could freeze/reuse the object. If so, all routes would collide into one children map — a critical routing bug that unit tests with a single route would not catch. Please verify the helper's implementation allocates per call. Medium confidence, since I cannot read the helper here.

claim: Type safety of `#children` may be weakened if `createNullObject()` is typed as `any`/`object` rather than a generic returning the annotated type.
rationale: `Object.create(null)` returns `any`, which assigns to `Record<string, Node>` silently. A helper typed as `(): object` would be a compile error, while one typed `(): any` keeps the same (weak) behavior. Ideally it should be generic (`createNullObject<T extends object = Record<string, unknown>>(): T`) so callers keep the declared type. Low-to-medium confidence; worth confirming the signature so this doesn't silently widen/narrow the type at other call sites too.

claim: Behavior change risk: if `createNullObject` does anything beyond `Object.create(null)` (e.g. returns a `Proxy`, a `Map`-backed shim, or a prototype-frozen object), hot-path property access/`in` checks on `#children` could change semantics or performance.
rationale: `#children` is on the router's insert/lookup hot path and is accessed with plain indexing and likely `in`/`hasOwnProperty`-free lookups that rely on a bare null-prototype object. Any wrapper would alter both semantics (e.g. `__proto__` handling) and V8 inline-cache behavior. Low confidence — flagging only because the substitution hides the actual allocation from this file.

claim: The budget/indexing check (`if (scanBudget < 0) { ... indexChildrenByKey ... }`) is moved inside the new `else` branch, so it is skipped entirely whenever the first old child matches.
rationale: Previously this ran on every iteration of the `else if` branch. Now a run of head-matches never re-evaluates it. This is probably benign because `scanBudget` can only go negative inside the `else` branch and is reset to `Infinity` in the same block, so it should never be negative on entry to a fast-path iteration. Worth verifying the initialization of `scanBudget` outside this hunk: if it can start at or below 0, the keyed index would never be built and the linear-scan fallback would be used forever. Medium confidence this is harmless.

claim: The child-matching predicate is now duplicated: once inline as `isMatchFirst` and once inside `findIndex`; the two copies must stay semantically identical.
rationale: I compared both forms and they currently agree (NodeString<->NodeString; keyed -> key+tag; unkeyed -> tag only). But this duplication means any future change to the matching rules applied to only one copy will silently produce wrong node reuse, which is hard to debug. Extracting a shared `const matches = (c) => ...` used by both the head test and `findIndex` would remove the risk. High confidence this is a real hazard, though not a bug today.

claim: On a fast-path miss, index 0 is compared twice (once by `isMatchFirst`, then again by `findIndex`, which starts at 0), and the extra comparison is not charged against `scanBudget`.
rationale: Worst case now does N+1 comparisons instead of N, and `scanBudget` is no longer an exact count of comparisons performed, slightly delaying the switch to the keyed index for adversarial reorderings. Low impact; could be avoided by starting the search at index 1 and adjusting the returned index.

claim: `oldVChildren[0]` is read and passed to `isNodeString` without any guard against a hole or `undefined` entry.
rationale: `oldVChildren.length > 0` does not guarantee element 0 is a defined node (sparse array or `undefined` placeholder); `isNodeString` typically dereferences a property and would throw a TypeError. The pre-existing `findIndex` predicate had the same exposure, so this is not a clear regression, but the new code dereferences the head unconditionally for every child. Low confidence this is reachable; flagged only because `first` is used with no null check.

claim: The new `jsonContentTypeRegex` only accepts the `application/...` tree, so common JSON content types such as `text/json` (and `text/x-json`) that the middleware may previously have pretty-printed (or that callers expect to be pretty-printed) will now be skipped silently.
rationale: Regex is anchored with `^application\/`. If the prior implementation used something like `startsWith('application/json')` this is not a regression, but if it checked `includes('json')` or `text/json` it is. Medium confidence that this is an intentional narrowing, but worth confirming against the tests.

claim: The structured-suffix prefix class `[a-z0-9._-]+` is narrower than the RFC 6838 subtype token set and does not allow `+`, so valid types like `application/vnd.foo+bar+json` or subtypes containing `!`/`#`/`$`/`^` etc. will not be recognized as JSON.
rationale: RFC 6838 restricted-name characters include `!#$&^_+.-` and digits/letters; nested structured suffixes exist in the wild. Low-to-medium confidence this matters in practice, but it is a real coverage gap of the matcher.

claim: The regex requires the media type to start at index 0 with no tolerance for leading whitespace, and the lookahead `(?=$|[;\s])` does not accept `,`. A header value such as ` application/json` (leading space, which some proxies/frameworks produce) or a comma-separated value list will not match.
rationale: Header values are usually trimmed by the runtime's Headers implementation, so this is likely harmless, but if the value is read from a raw object/init it can retain whitespace. Low confidence, but cheap to guard with a `\s*` prefix or a `.trim()` before testing.

claim: The constant is declared at module scope but is not exported and no usage appears in this hunk; if the accompanying call site was not updated, this is dead code and will trip `noUnusedLocals`/lint.
rationale: Cannot see the rest of the file in this hunk, so confidence is low — flagged only so the reviewer verifies the regex is actually wired into the content-type check that replaced the previous string comparison.

claim: The newly added `chUaHighEntropyValues` does not appear to correspond to a real Permissions-Policy feature; the client-hint policy tokens are `ch-ua`, `ch-ua-arch`, `ch-ua-bitness`, `ch-ua-full-version`, `ch-ua-full-version-list`, `ch-ua-form-factor(s)`, `ch-ua-mobile`, `ch-ua-model`, `ch-ua-platform`, `ch-ua-platform-version`, `ch-ua-wow64`. `getHighEntropyValues()` is a JS API, not a policy-controlled feature.
rationale: If the token is not registered, the middleware will serialize `ch-ua-high-entropy-values=(...)` into the Permissions-Policy header. Browsers ignore unknown directives, but it silently gives users a false sense that they have restricted high-entropy client hints, and some strict header validators/linters flag unknown tokens. Medium confidence — worth verifying against the spec registry before shipping, and if a name was intended here it may be `chUaFormFactors`.

claim: This adds the key only to the type union; the camelCase→kebab-case mapping and any runtime feature list/docs/tests must be updated in lockstep or the new option will be accepted by the type checker but produce no (or wrong) output.
rationale: Many implementations derive the header token from the key via a generic camelCase-to-kebab regex, in which case this is fine, but some keep an explicit lookup table or a documented feature list. Since this hunk touches only the type, the change is incomplete if a runtime table exists. Low-to-medium confidence without seeing the serialization code — please confirm `chUaHighEntropyValues` actually serializes to `ch-ua-high-entropy-values` and that docs/tests were updated.

claim: Hoisting `allowHeadersStr` out of the request handler risks dropping the per-request fallback to the `Access-Control-Request-Headers` request header (and its `Vary: Access-Control-Request-Headers` append) in the preflight path.
rationale: In the original CORS logic the allowed-headers value is normally computed per request as `opts.allowHeaders?.length ? opts.allowHeaders : c.req.header('Access-Control-Request-Headers')?.split(...)`, and the `Vary` header is appended only when that fallback applies. A precomputed constant string can only represent the configured case; if the call site was changed to use `allowHeadersStr` unconditionally, reflected request headers and the `Vary` entry would silently disappear, breaking preflights for clients that send custom headers. I cannot see the consumer in this hunk, so this is a suspicion worth verifying rather than a confirmed bug.

claim: The header strings are now snapshotted at middleware-construction time, so mutations to the caller-supplied `allowHeaders`/`exposeHeaders` arrays after `cors(...)` is called no longer take effect.
rationale: Previously the arrays were joined on each request, so a caller pushing into the array they passed in would see the change. Now the join happens once. This is an unlikely but real behavior change for existing callers; low confidence that anyone depends on it, but it is a genuine semantic difference introduced by the hoist.

claim: Empty arrays are mapped to `undefined` rather than an empty string; make sure downstream code distinguishes `undefined` (omit header) from `''` the same way the previous inline check did.
rationale: `opts.exposeHeaders?.length ? ... : undefined` means a configured-but-empty list produces `undefined`. If the consumer previously wrote the header whenever `exposeHeaders` was truthy (an empty array is truthy) or used a `!== undefined` vs truthiness check inconsistently, the emitted headers could change. Moderate confidence this is fine, but the truthiness semantics changed shape and deserve a check at the use site.

claim: Adding 'Accept-Query' only to the `RequestHeader` type union may leave a companion runtime list (or a parallel `ResponseHeader` union) out of sync.
rationale: Header-name modules like this commonly pair the literal union with a runtime array/Set used for validation or completion, and often split request vs response header unions. The diff only touches this one union; if a sibling constant or the response-header union exists, it will no longer cover 'Accept-Query'. Note also that Accept-Query (like the neighboring Accept-Patch/Accept-Post) is defined as a *response* header advertising QUERY support, so placing it in `RequestHeader` may be semantically wrong depending on how this type is consumed. Low confidence — I can only see this hunk, so this needs verification against the rest of the file/module.

claim: The comparator can return a non-zero value when `a` and `b` are the same wildcard string, violating the `compare(x, x) === 0` contract.
rationale: With the new expression, `compareKey('.*', '.*')` returns 1 and `compareKey(TAIL, TAIL)` returns -1 instead of 0. In practice the inputs are usually distinct object keys so this may never be hit, but an inconsistent comparator can yield implementation-defined ordering in `Array.prototype.sort` and makes the function unsafe for any future caller that can pass equal keys. Cheap to fix with an explicit `a === b ? 0 : ...` guard. Medium confidence it is currently unreachable, hence low severity.

claim: Only the `a`-side branch was updated; the `b`-side branch still returns a constant, so the antisymmetry of the new wildcard ordering is accidental rather than explicit.
rationale: `compareKey(TAIL, ONLY)` falls into the first branch and returns 1, while `compareKey(ONLY, TAIL)` returns -1, which happens to be consistent. But the `else if` here is never reached when `a` is a wildcard, so the rule 'ONLY precedes TAIL' lives in exactly one place with no mirrored logic; reordering these branches later would silently break antisymmetry. Moderate confidence this is a robustness concern rather than a live bug.

claim: Swapping the relative order of `.*` and the tail wildcard changes regex alternation priority and may make tail-wildcard routes unreachable.
rationale: These sorted keys are joined into a regular expression alternation, where the first matching alternative wins. `.*` matches every remaining input (including the empty string), so placing it before the tail wildcard means the tail-wildcard alternative can never be reached for any input the only-wildcard node also accepts. Previously both wildcards were pushed to the end by an (inconsistent) comparator; now the order deterministically favors `.*`. This can change which handler wins for paths matched by both wildcard kinds. Not fully certain of the intended precedence since it depends on how the node tree builds the alternation, but a test covering a path matched by both wildcards is warranted.

claim: The new JSDoc claims `options.realm` "Defaults to the request URL" — this should be verified against the actual implementation, since a URL default for a `realm` challenge parameter is unusual and easy to get wrong (e.g. the code may default to an empty string, the origin, or the full `c.req.url` including query string).
rationale: The diff only adds documentation; the implementation is not visible in this hunk. If the real default differs, the doc misleads callers about the emitted `WWW-Authenticate` header. Additionally, defaulting the realm to the full request URL can leak internal path/query information to unauthenticated clients. Medium confidence — cannot confirm without seeing the implementation, but the claim is specific enough to warrant cross-checking.

claim: `options.realm` is documented as `{string}` only, unlike sibling options (`keys`, `jwks_uri`) which also accept a `(ctx: Context) => ...` resolver; also, a realm containing `"` or non-ASCII characters would produce a malformed `WWW-Authenticate` header unless the implementation escapes it.
rationale: If the implementation accepts a function form, the type annotation is incomplete; if it only accepts a string, unescaped quotes in a caller-supplied realm are a header-injection / malformed-challenge risk. Low-to-medium confidence, since escaping may be handled where the header is built.

claim: The documented default for `options.allowMethods` now includes `'QUERY'`; if the actual `defaults`/`opts` object in this file still initializes `allowMethods` to `['GET', 'HEAD', 'PUT', 'POST', 'DELETE', 'PATCH']`, the JSDoc is now misleading and will surface a wrong default in editor tooltips and generated docs.
rationale: The hunk only shows the comment, not the implementation, so I cannot verify the runtime default from the diff. Doc/implementation drift on a default value is a plausible issue worth confirming: the corresponding literal in the middleware body (and the Preflight `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` header it produces) should be updated in the same change. Moderate confidence — this is likely part of a larger PR that also changes the default, but if the default array was not touched the documentation is simply wrong.

claim: Adding `QUERY` to the default `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` broadens the advertised method set for every existing caller that does not pass `allowMethods` explicitly.
rationale: If the implementation default really changed, preflight responses for all existing users will now advertise the (still-draft) HTTP QUERY method without opt-in. That is a silent behavior change for existing callers and may trip strict security scanners or proxies that reject unknown methods. Low-to-moderate confidence that this matters in practice, but it is worth an explicit note in the changelog/release notes.

claim: `sha256` from `../../utils/crypto` resolves to `string | null` (it returns null when `crypto.subtle` is unavailable or digesting fails); if the new code uses its result directly as the query digest cache key, a null digest can collapse distinct request bodies onto one cache entry or produce the literal key "null".
rationale: Hono's `utils/crypto` `sha256`/`createHash` helpers are declared as `Promise<string | null>` and silently return null on unsupported runtimes. Any consumer must null-check and fall back to bypassing the cache. I can't see the usage site in this hunk, so this is a flag to verify, but it is a common bug with this helper.

claim: `cloneRawRequest` is a runtime (value) import from `../../request` into a middleware module that previously only had type-only imports; this adds a hard runtime dependency and a potential circular-import / bundle-size regression.
rationale: All prior imports here are `import type`, so this file previously compiled away to zero runtime deps. `src/request` is a core module that may transitively import context/types, so a cycle is plausible and would surface as an undefined binding at module init. Moderate confidence — worth checking the import graph.

claim: `defaultMaxQueryBodySize = 64 * 1024` is a byte threshold, but if it is enforced against `content-length` only (or against a decoded string length), chunked requests without `content-length` and multi-byte unicode bodies can bypass the guard and be fully buffered.
rationale: A size cap is only effective if enforced on actual consumed byte length while streaming. Requests without `content-length` are the classic hole. Low-to-moderate confidence since the enforcement site isn't in this hunk, but the constant's introduction makes it worth verifying.

claim: The synthetic cache key path `'/.hono/cache'` plus fixed query parameters can collide with real application routes sharing the same Cache Storage namespace, and the user-supplied cache key must be URL-encoded when embedded as a query value.
rationale: If the app itself serves `/.hono/cache`, or a user cache key contains `&`/`#`/non-ASCII and is concatenated rather than set via `URLSearchParams`, keys can be forged or mis-parsed, causing cross-entry cache poisoning. Moderate confidence — depends on how the URL is assembled below this hunk.

claim: The `CacheKeyRequest` union allows `method: 'QUERY'`, but the Web Cache API rejects non-GET requests for `cache.put`/`match` (without `ignoreMethod`); constructing a real `Request` with method `QUERY` for storage would throw a TypeError at runtime.
rationale: `cache.put()`/`match()` throw for non-GET request objects. The design presumably rewrites to a GET on the synthetic path, which would be correct, but the union hints the method may be carried onto the real Request. Low confidence, but a runtime throw here is a hard failure and cheap to verify.

claim: `queryRepresentationMetadataHeaders` omits `content-length`/`content-digest` while including `content-location`; if this list defines which request headers feed the body digest, semantically different QUERY bodies with identical listed headers could share a cache entry.
rationale: Representation metadata affecting body interpretation should be hashed with the body; `content-location` does not affect interpretation while length does. Low confidence — may be intentional per the QUERY draft, but the selection deserves a second look.

claim: Adding `QUERY` only to this `If-None-Match: *` branch likely leaves the rest of the middleware inconsistent about the QUERY method.
rationale: The etag middleware typically gates other behavior on the request method as well (e.g. whether an ETag is generated/attached at all, or which responses are eligible for 304 / cache handling elsewhere in this file or in the cache middleware). If those checks still only list GET/HEAD, a QUERY request can now receive a 304 in the `*` case while never getting an ETag header (or vice-versa) in the ordinary flow, producing asymmetric behavior. Worth verifying every `method === 'GET' || method === 'HEAD'` site in the package and factoring them into one shared predicate/set. Medium confidence — depends on code outside this hunk.

claim: The non-`*` branch (`etagMatches`) still applies to any method, so the new method allow-list is only enforced for `If-None-Match: *`.
rationale: Per RFC 9110, `If-None-Match` on a non-safe method that fails should yield 412, and 304 is only valid for GET/HEAD (now GET/HEAD/QUERY). Here a POST/PUT with a concrete `If-None-Match` value that matches will still be turned into a 304 below. This is pre-existing rather than introduced by the diff, but the change draws attention to the asymmetry and is a good time to align both branches on the same method predicate. Moderate confidence about the spec mismatch, low confidence it's in scope for this change.

claim: Method comparison uses raw uppercase string literals; a lowercase or non-normalized `c.req.method` would silently skip the QUERY case.
rationale: Hono normally surfaces `method` exactly as sent by the client/runtime; HTTP methods are case-sensitive so uppercase comparison is technically correct, but if any adapter (test harness, custom fetch mock) passes `query`, the branch quietly falls through to a full 200 response instead of 304. Low confidence this matters in practice, but using a shared constant/set of allowed methods would make it robust and self-documenting.

claim: `{}` is not assignable to the generic type `E['Bindings']` without a cast, so this likely fails type-checking (or silently widens/erases the binding type).
rationale: `E['Bindings']` is an unresolved generic indexed access; TypeScript only accepts an initializer that is assignable to every possible instantiation. If `Bindings` is e.g. `{ COUNTER: DurableObjectNamespace }`, the empty object literal does not satisfy it. If it does compile today it is only because of a looser constraint, and at runtime `c.env.COUNTER` is now `undefined` rather than a type error surface. Fairly confident this needs `= {} as E['Bindings']`.

claim: A field initializer can be immediately overwritten by the constructor if it unconditionally does `this.env = options.env`, making the default ineffective when `options.env` is undefined.
rationale: Class field initializers run before the constructor body. Unless the constructor guards with `options.env ?? {}` / `if (options.env)`, passing `{ env: undefined }` (or an options object without `env`) will set `this.env` back to `undefined` and defeat the purpose of this change. Worth verifying the Context constructor assignment; I can't see it in this hunk.

claim: Behavior change: `c.env` is now a truthy empty object instead of `undefined` for callers that never supply bindings.
rationale: Existing middleware/adapters that branch on `if (c.env)` or `c.env === undefined` (common in non-workers runtimes like Node/Deno where bindings are not provided) will now take the opposite branch. Also each Context construction allocates a fresh object per request, a small but per-request cost on a hot path. Moderate confidence this affects real callers.
